source.title: What Money Was
source.summary: The Islamic monetary system as it actually functioned: gold dinars, silver dirhams, sarrafs, and the institutions that held it together.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: In 696 CE, Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan made a revolutionary decision: he minted the first purely Islamic gold dinar, replacing Byzantine and Sassanid coins across the caliphate. This wasn't just currency reform. It was a declaration of monetary sovereignty. The Islamic bimetallic system that emerged had standardized weights (the mithqal), quality control through the muhtasib, proto-forex markets run by sarrafs, and mint networks spanning three continents. This episode examines how the system actually worked, where it succeeded, and where it struggled, from Mamluk debasement to silver-gold ratio instability. The key insight: Islamic civilization didn't just have money. It had a monetary system with rules, institutions, and oversight.
